# Calibration corpus, English, continued (VER-11, Latin script). The full Latin run reads
# passages-en.txt and then this file, so its first 60 passages are the good candidates.
# passages-en.txt stays as the VER-07 mini run used it: its bytes are that run's evidence identity.
# Written for this project and quoted from nowhere; each passage has a name, a number and a clause.
# One passage per line. Do not reorder.
The lighthouse keeper at Gannet Point, a widower called Osric Penhale, painted the stairs a different colour every spring for twenty years.
When the fair came to Mardle Green, the twins spent all eight of their pennies on the first stall and spent the rest of the day watching everyone else.
Wilhelmina Strand kept bees on the roof of the post office, and the postmaster claimed the letters arrived sweeter in the summer months.
The night train to Harrowgate stopped at four small stations, but the guard, a cheerful man named Fennick, announced each one as if it were a capital city.
Old Mrs Tolley at Linden Row baked nine loaves every Friday, though she lived alone and never once explained who ate the other eight.
The quarry above Stenbury closed in the long winter of that year, and the men who had cut stone for thirty years learned to cut hedges instead.
Barnaby Quill wrote the parish newsletter for eleven years, and in all that time he printed only one correction, which was itself mistaken.
The well in the square at Ormsby never froze, even in the hardest frost, and the children believed a warm river ran somewhere far beneath it.
At the end of every term, the headmistress of Coldharbour School read out the names of all sixty pupils, and she never needed to look at a list.
Jonas Merriwether bought the derelict cinema on Station Road for five hundred pounds, and for a decade he showed the same three films in rotation.
The tide at Saltmarsh came in faster than strangers expected, and the coastguard rescued at least two picnics a summer from the rising water.
Rosalind Thackeray grew roses for the county show, and she won second prize twelve years running, always behind the same quiet neighbour.
The bakery on Fuller Street opened at five, but the queue began forming at half past four, because the first tray of buns was always the best.
Every autumn the geese flew over Hollins Moor in their thousands, and the shepherd, a man named Corwen, stopped work to count them from the ridge.
The postbox at Ditchley Corner was emptied twice a day, though nobody could remember the last time anyone had actually posted a letter in it.
Mabel Fairweather taught the village choir for forty years, and she said the secret of good singing was to listen harder than you sang.
The canal boat called the Patient Heron carried coal to Wexford Basin for half a century, and it was never once late, though it was never early.
On the coldest night of the winter, the pub at Brackenford stayed open until dawn, and seven travellers slept beside its fire on the stone floor.
Lucian Abernathy repaired violins in a workshop above the chemist, and he claimed that every instrument told him what was wrong with it.
The clock on the town hall at Penmorrow ran ten minutes slow, and the council decided it was cheaper to change the train timetable than the clock.
Ivy Coulthard walked her three dogs along the cliff path every morning, and the dogs knew the way so well that she sometimes simply followed them.
The cricket ground at Ashby Parva flooded every spring, and the club played its first six matches of the season on the vicarage lawn instead.
Ambrose Tull sold umbrellas from a cart on Market Hill, and in a dry year he sold sunshades from the same cart without changing the sign.
The ferryman at Rookwater charged one penny to cross the river and two to come back, because, he said, the return journey was uphill.
Clementine Ashdown learned Latin at seventy, and by eighty she was correcting the inscriptions on half the gravestones in the churchyard.
The stationmaster at Little Hembury grew tomatoes along the platform, and passengers on the slow train were allowed to pick one each in August.
Gideon Farrow kept a diary for fifty years, and when his grandson finally read it, he found that every single entry began with the weather.
The village of Thornleigh had one telephone, kept in the shop, and when it rang the shopkeeper ran into the street to shout the caller's name.
Agatha Moorcroft swam in the lake at Elderwater every morning of the year, and in January she broke the ice herself with a garden spade.
The orchestra at Kingsbridge rehearsed in a barn, and the cows in the next field grew so calm that the farmer offered to pay the violinists.
Percival Dunne ran the lending library at Woolcombe for thirty years, and he could tell you who had borrowed any book by the smell of its pages.
The road over Ravenscar Pass closed every December, and the four farms beyond it laid in flour, candles and patience until the spring.
Winifred Hale made jam from the brambles along the railway line, and she sold every jar to the driver of the nine o'clock goods train.
The church at Upper Sedley had a weathervane shaped like a fish, and the old men swore it pointed toward rain more truly than any forecast.
Cornelius Webb built model ships inside bottles, and after fifteen years he had filled every windowsill in the cottage and started on the stairs.
The harbour at Polgarra froze only once in living memory, and the fishermen still argue about whether anybody really walked across it.
Hester Lindqvist ran the telephone exchange at Grindley for twenty-six years, and she knew every secret in the valley and kept every one.
The old mill race at Stowford still ran, though the mill had gone, and the children floated paper boats down it to a pool beneath the willows.
